02af481f0f6d403d: KUALA LUMPUR: Caring for ageing parents while raising children of their own places a double burden on some families, as medical bills, professional care and daily expenses will stretch household budgets.
Therefore, the 2027 Budget has raised hopes of greater support, but elderly care service providers and senior citizens say effective implementation will be key to easing the strain.
National Secretary of the Association of Residential Aged Care Operators of Malaysia (Agecope) Fong Muntoh described the 2027 Budget as a long-awaited breakthrough after 27 years in the business.
"This is the first time I have seen a budget bring together so many meaningful measures for seniors and the families supporting them.
"The government has taken a very positive step."
Fong said the allocation of more than RM40 million to train 8,000 people for the elderly care sector could help address the shortage of caregivers.
He also cited the reduction in service tax from 8 per cent to 6 per cent and the exemption for elderly care fees of up to RM96,000 a year as measures that could ease the financial burden on families.
The planned National Integrated Care Centres of Excellence in Penang and Sarawak, which were expected to support training, research and elderly care, were another encouraging development, he said.
Fong added that the measures could also ease the pressure on the "sandwich generation", whose members must care for ageing parents while supporting their own families.
"Now we await the implementation. The announcements are good. Let us hope the delivery is just as good," he said.
Senior care activist Tony Lian, who runs several charitable care centres, said elderly care should be a shared responsibility rather than a burden borne by individuals and their families.
He said the RM1.3 billion allocation for Bantuan Warga Emas, tax relief for family caregivers and investment in care facilities and training reflected greater recognition of the needs of the elderly.
"These measures recognise that ageing is not just an individual or family responsibility, but a shared responsibility that requires government and community support.
"We are an ageing nation. A dignified old age should be a right, not a privilege.
"The 2027 Budget helps make that a reality," he said.
Lian, however, hopes more can be done to help poor, homeless elderly people found abandoned on the streets and in hospitals.

For 65-year-old Nur Mastura Mohd Khalid, the proposed monthly withdrawal option for Employees Provident Fund (EPF) savings could help retirees manage their finances and budget for daily necessities, medical bills and other expenses.
She also said the reduction in service tax on elderly care services could ease the burden on primary caregivers and families paying for professional care.
However, she said that the measures must provide meaningful relief to retirees and families facing a burden who had to grapple with increased costs.
Beyond financial assistance, C.K. Leong, 67, called for safer and more accessible public facilities to help the elderly remain active and independent.

She said elderly-friendly facilities should be available in every neighbourhood — including safer walkways, accessible parks with elderly-friendly exercise machines and affordable day-care centres — particularly for low-income households.
Leong said poorly designed pavements and high kerbs could discourage older people from walking and exercising.
She proposed installing lifts in older walk-up apartment blocks, with the government and apartment owners sharing the costs.
She said owners should be allowed to use their EPF savings to cover part of their contribution, subject to approval.
Meanwhile, P. Inahsav, 57, said private-sector retirees risked being overlooked despite efforts to strengthen support for senior citizens.

She suggested the proposed minimum monthly pension of RM1,350 as a positive move, but questioned whether it would cover daily necessities and healthcare, particularly for elderly people without family support.
Inahsav said retirees without government pensions could face financial pressure as the cost of living and medical expenses continued to rise.
She called for the private-sector retirement age to be raised to 65, allowing healthy people with insufficient savings to continue working and build their retirement funds.
"Covid-19 took a hit on most people's savings, EPF and livelihood.
"If politicians can work until their 70s or 80s, why can't ordinary citizens who are struggling to make ends meet continue working until 65, especially when they are healthy and able?"
She added that those financially prepared for retirement should retain the option to retire earlier, while others should have the opportunity to work longer.

9b39341c989035a9: CITIES are rarely still. They grow, spread and reshape themselves, with roads, buildings and neighbourhoods changing the landscape.
But beyond the concrete and glass, another story is unfolding — in the forests that sit alongside the city and remain closely intertwined with the lives of the people who call it home.

That relationship is at the heart of The Line: Beyond the Forest's Edge — a new exhibition by Bank Negara Malaysia Museum and Art Gallery (BNM MAG), featuring acclaimed photographer Ian Teh's award-winning The Line series.

Running until April 4, 2027, the exhibition looks at the evolving relationship between Greater Kuala Lumpur and its surrounding forests, documenting the city's urbanisation and transformation over the past five decades from a bird's-eye perspective.
But this is more than a collection of photographs about a changing skyline.

Through 51 photographs, an audio piece, a video documentary screened in a dark room and an immersive 360° virtual reality experience, Teh invites visitors to look at familiar landscapes differently — and, perhaps, to notice what lies beyond the city's increasingly shifting boundaries.
The work recently received the Sagamihara Photography Asia Award, but for Teh, The Line is rooted in something more personal than recognition.
He describes it as a "deeply personal love letter" to his country of birth, centred on Greater Kuala Lumpur and its forests.

For him, the city and the forest are the exhibition's two "main characters". One represents the lived reality of urban life; the other offers a glimpse of the remarkable, sometimes almost unfamiliar beauty that exists right on our doorstep.
And the two, he says, are inextricably connected.
PAUSE AND LOOK
As the city continues to face the pressures of growth and climate change, the exhibition touches on issues like climate adaptation, land use, biodiversity conservation and sustainable mobility.

BNM MAG director Noreen Zulkepli says the exhibition is intended to encourage visitors to think about how development and nature can thrive together, while reflecting the central bank's efforts to incorporate sustainability considerations into economic policies that support long-term growth and resilience.

For visitors, however, the idea need not feel quite so weighty. Perhaps it's simply an invitation to pause and look at a city many of us know intimately, and at the natural world that exists beside it.

Because the places we inhabit are never just buildings, roads and skylines. They are also the trees beyond the expressway, the forests at the edge of the city and the natural spaces woven quietly into our everyday lives.

2858ffd6b93ec192: JOHOR BARU: A Malaysian plantation group and several Singapore-linked business interests have been identified as companies linked to Indonesian concessions where fire hotspots were detected.
Indonesian authorities have yet to disclose the identities or nationalities of the 19 companies investigated over fires affecting 11,047ha across seven provinces.
A report by Greenpeace Indonesia, Greenpeace Malaysia and Pantau Gambut identified at least one Malaysian company alongside four concessions linked to Singapore-based business interests.
The findings, released on Oct 5, however, did not point fingers at them for starting the fires in Sumatra and West Kalimantan, or committing any offence.
Indonesian Consul-General in Johor Baru Sigit Suryantoro Widiyanto said they identified 57 businesses across eight provinces in their enforcement crackdown.
Indonesia's environment ministry enforcement authorities had linked the businesses to open burning covering 33,514ha.
Authorities recorded 97 police reports involving corporations, while criminal investigations were under way against 46 suspects, including five companies.
The forestry ministry had imposed administrative sanctions on 26 companies, including revoking five permits, suspending 13 and issuing written warnings or restoration orders to eight.

On Thursday, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto agreed to take measures to address the worsening haze, as Malaysia renewed calls for stronger regional cooperation.

Meanwhile, Sari Wilson-Pohan, an Indonesian who has lived in Johor since 2014, said she was embarrassed and saddened by what she viewed as a lack of urgency by Indonesia in addressing the fires. Both her sons attend school in Johor and her husband works in Singapore.

"Regardless of who owns the companies, Indonesia must put humanity first. Protecting people, the environment and our future should always come before protecting big businesses," she told the New Straits Times.
She said she had submitted an open letter to Prabowo urging decisive action and accountability.
"Enough is enough. People must come before profits."
98cb599b7040702c: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump demanded that Volodymyr Zelensky halt attacks on Russian oil refineries and suggested he should consider stepping aside as Ukraine’s president, escalating a fight centered on securing more diesel supplies for the US ahead of the midterm elections.

“I think it’s time for Ukraine to get a new president,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Saturday as he unleashed an angry critique of Zelensky, saying Ukraine needs a leader “who can make a deal” with Russia.
“There’s plenty of targets,” Trump said. “Don’t hit refineries.”
Zelensky previously blasted the US decision to help release Russian diesel fuel into the global markets, which includes a Treasury waiver for some sanctioned Russian fuel.

Trump said Friday he was working with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the diesel release, upending years of sanctions as the White House seeks ways to tame soaring fuel prices ahead of the Nov 3 elections. Zelensky quickly complained that the move will give Russia more resources to continue the war.

On Friday, Ukrainian negotiators left a day early than planned from Miami, where they’d been talking with Trump envoys on ways to end Russia’s full-scale of invasion of its neighbor. Hours later, at least 20 people were killed when Russia struck residential buildings in Ukraine.

Trump announced a series of cargoes beginning this month that he said would initially total about 13.5 million barrels, initially. A Kremlin statement cited Putin as saying that Russia’s ready “to supply oil and petroleum products to the US and global markets.”

On Saturday, Russia partially lifted its ban on diesel exports, allowing 500,000 metric tons of fuel to reach international markets. The government didn’t say when the 500,000 tons would be shipped or whether additional export volumes could be authorized.

Following the US announcement, Germany and the UK issued statements confirming their commitment to maintaining strong sanctions on Russia. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham spoke with Zelensky on Satruday and will meet him in person in the coming days, according to a Downing Street spokesperson, who reaffirmed London’s complete support for Ukraine.

Diesel, the fuel often dubbed the workhorse of the global economy, has been thrust into the spotlight as a massive supply crunch sent pump prices to records and stoked concerns over energy-driven inflation.
Democrats were swift to condemn Trump’s deal to facilitate the Russian sale of energy supplies, arguing that it would help give Moscow much-needed funds for their war effort in Ukraine.

Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania said he plans to introduce a bill that would block any purchases of Russian oil. “It will be called the ‘Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act,’” he wrote in a post on X.

Senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican from Alaska, also blasted Trump’s decision, noting that Congress passed legislation that empowers the US president to impose tariffs on countries that purchase Russian petroleum products, which he signed.
“We can discuss Russia’s return to global energy markets once the war is over, but in the meantime, we need to cut off everything fueling it,” she wrote on social media.
Trump claimed during his reelection campaign that he could swiftly end the war and has clashed repeatedly with Zelensky since returning to the White House in 2025.

In February 2025, Trump questioned Zelensky’s legitimacy as Ukrainian leader, calling him a “dictator” who was balking at holding elections in wartime Ukraine. The following week, the two leaders argued face to face in Oval Office during an extraordinary public blowup over their clashing perspectives on the war, including the roles of Putin and former US President Joe Biden. Trump has wavered hot and cold over Zelensky since.
f319eb990ebc412d: PETALING JAYA: Scratch men’s doubles pair Aaron Tai-Yap Roy King produced another stunning performance to defeat higher-ranked opponents and reached the final of the Arctic Open, a World Tour Super 500 championships.

Despite playing together for the first time, the Malaysian duo played confidently to defeat world No 32 Danish pair Christian Faust Kjaer-Rasmus Kjaer 21-14, 21-16 in just 37 minutes at the Energia Areena in Vantaa, Finland last night.
The duo will next face either Taiwanese pair Lai Po Yu-Tsai Fu Cheng or Julien Maio-William Villeger from France.
This is the Malaysian duo’s fourth giant-killing feat in the championships after having beaten all higher-ranked pairs so far in straight games.

After an upset win over their world No 24 compatriots Nur Azriyn Ayub-Tan Wee Kiong in the opening round, Aaron-Roy King went on to beat world No 21 ranked Taiwanese brothers Lee Fang Chih-Lee Fang Jen in the last 16.
They then defeated top Thai duo Peeratchai Sukphun-Pakkapon Teeraratsakul in the quarter-final.
Winners of the doubles titles in all categories will get a prize money of US$39,500 (RM160,654) while the runners-up take home US$19,000 (RM77,277). All semi-finalists earn US$7,000 (RM28,470) each.
9ad8e8c4631e504e: KUALA LUMPUR: For young Malaysians who give their time to help others, RM100 may cover the cost of getting to a volunteering session, but the satisfaction of making a difference is what keeps them going.

The proposed Budi Belia e-wallet incentive under the 2027 Budget could draw more youths into community work, particularly students who struggle to meet expenses, but those already volunteering say sustaining their interest will take more than financial rewards.

Universiti Putra Malaysia (UPM) veterinary student Yaashinii Naaidu Sri Sivabalasundram, 22, who volunteers at the Furry Kids Safe Haven dog shelter in Rantau, Negri Sembilan, said the money could help cover transport, meals and other expenses.
"Although it may not be a huge amount, it can serve as a good starting point to encourage youth participation," she said.
But Yaashinii said she would continue volunteering even without the incentive because of her commitment to animal welfare.
"I would have volunteered anyway because I genuinely care about animal welfare and enjoy contributing to a meaningful cause," she said.
For Nor Arisha Natasha Mustapar, 25, the incentive could help youths take their first step into volunteering, even if money was initially their main motivation.

The UPM graduate, who works at Sanofi-Aventis (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd, has joined initiatives including delivering aid to B40 households through Yayasan Belia Malaysia's Harapan Ramadan 2026 programme, serving food with Feeding the Needy in Chow Kit and teaching underprivileged students through Tuisyen Madani.

"I see it less as a payment for their service and more as a small incentive to encourage them to take their first step," she said, adding that the experience could help them develop empathy and a stronger sense of social responsibility.
For Nor Syazlin Ishak, 22, who has volunteered with Feeding the Needy, BeKind Malaysia and Special Kids Therapy Centre, the value of volunteering lies in the human connection it creates.

"It is not only about providing food but also about making people feel valued, respected and cared for," she said, adding that simple gestures, such as wishing someone a good night or asking them to take care, could make a difference.
However, Nur Durrah Annisa Rusidi, 23, said getting young people involved was only half the challenge, as keeping them engaged required meaningful opportunities to contribute.
"We need to make volunteering meaningful, not just financially attractive," she said.
Durrah, who previously volunteered through her university's organisation, Majlis Mahasiswa Anak Perlis, is working towards establishing a non-governmental organisation, GenzPerlis.
She said young people should be trusted with greater responsibility, including leading projects and participating in decision-making.
"Give us the platform, let us lead projects, involve us in decision-making and take our voices seriously.

The volunteers called for Budi Belia to support a wider range of causes, including animal welfare, environmental conservation and community service, while creating more opportunities for sustained involvement rather than one-off activities.
Yaashinii said this would allow youths to build lasting connections with the causes they support.
Meanwhile, Durrah said "the real success of Budi Belia would be when young people continue showing up, even after the incentive is gone".
Syazlin, who developed an interest in volunteering while in secondary school, said the experience had broadened her perspective and taught her to be more compassionate.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd
d23a976be95ad717: MALAYALEE heritage in Malaysia has, over generations, quietly folded itself into the larger Malaysian story. We've assimilated, adapted and, inevitably, changed. Yet some things stubbornly remain, and very often, they survive on the tongue.
A taste. A smell. A dish placed on the table that takes you somewhere before you quite understand why.
Reading Anitha Devi Pillai's What the Tongue Remembers, a collection of 11 stories about Malayalee women in Singapore, I kept thinking about my own mother's kitchen.

Pillai writes of women carrying secrets, making choices, enduring heartbreak and living with the silences that families sometimes keep for generations. Woven through their stories are recipes and dishes familiar to many Malayalee homes: pazham pori (banana fritters), unniappam, mambazha pulissery (mango yoghurt curry) and puttu with kadala (black chickpea) curry.
But these aren't simply dishes inserted between stories. Food becomes another way of remembering. And that was what caught me.

As I read, I began wondering about the stories behind my own mother's cooking. What memories sit inside her fish curry, with slices of mango from the tree growing in front of our house floating among the spices? What part of her own past survives in the puttu she makes, eaten with curry, which in turn has become part of my memories of home?
Perhaps this is what Anitha's title understands so beautifully. Sometimes the tongue remembers what the mind has long stopped thinking about.
PLOT TWISTS AND (UN)HAPPY ENDINGS
There are few straightforward lives in Anitha's world.

In The Blessing, the birth of a child isn't quite what it seems when Ambiga Iyer and Mareena Kurian find themselves in the same ward at Kandang Kerbau Hospital in Singapore. What begins as a story about motherhood gradually reveals something more complicated beneath it.

An Unusual Arrangement takes us much further back. Chellama is married at the tender age of 12 to 21-year-old Krishnan, who later leaves for Singapore in search of a better life. Eventually, Chellama and her children make their own journey to Singapore to join him during World War 2. What follows is a story shaped by migration, marriage and the choices women make within circumstances they didn't necessarily choose for themselves.

In Paper Mountains, mental illness casts its shadow over the relationship between a mother and daughter. For the daughter, there's another unsettling question to confront: is this something she, too, might carry with her into her own future?

Then there's Expiration Date, built around an intriguing premise in which marriages without children come with an actual expiry date. After 10 years, the marriage licence lapses and the couple must divorce. For Vashy and Lilly, the law forces them towards an unusual arrangement and raises the question of what, exactly, holds a marriage together.
Anitha clearly enjoys a plot twist, and there are plenty of them. Secrets surface, relationships shift and what appears to be one kind of story can suddenly become another.

At times, however, the plotting can become rather dense. There were stories I had to go back and read again, either to work out a relationship or to understand exactly how a revelation fitted into everything that had come before.
With so many turns packed into some of the narratives, the twists occasionally compete with the quieter emotional moments that are, for me, among the book's strengths.
Still, there's something compelling about these complicated women and their complicated lives. And running through all that drama is food, providing a kind of emotional anchor.
A recipe can appear almost deceptively simple beside a story filled with heartbreak, secrets and difficult choices. Yet perhaps that's the point. Life gets messy but the recipe remains.
MEMORIES AND STORIES
Reading these stories from Singapore also raises another question familiar to Malayalees in Malaysia. After generations away from Kerala, what exactly are we remembering?

Our food has travelled with us, but it hasn't remained untouched. Life in Malaysia, much like Singapore, has changed our recipes and introduced different ingredients, influences and tastes. Our palates have changed too. What my mother cooks may not taste exactly like what her mother cooked, just as what I remember as Malayalee food may be quite different from the food served in a Kerala home today.
But perhaps authenticity isn't really the point.

Recipes migrate because people migrate. They change because families change. A dish absorbs the place in which it is cooked, the ingredients available, the preferences of husbands and children and the improvisations of the woman standing over the stove.
And somewhere along the way, those adapted recipes become authentic to us.

That is what makes the food in What the Tongue Remembers so evocative. Anitha isn't merely serving up pazham pori, unniappam or mambazha pulissery. Through them, she gives us glimpses into the women who made, ate and remembered them.

And somewhere between her stories and recipes, I found myself thinking less about her kitchen and more about mine. About that mango tree outside the house… about my mother's fish curry… about puttu and curry on the table.
And, most of all, about the stories I may never have thought to ask her.

06e4bcd358f8324a: CHITRE: Residents near the epicentre of a major earthquake in southern Panama began cleaning up on Saturday, traumatised by the previous day's heavy shaking that left widespread damage but, so far, no reported deaths.
"This is something we've never seen before. We weren't prepared for this kind of event," said Aldulfo Quintero as he cleared debris from a store in Chitre, about 250km southwest of Panama City.
The 41-year-old told AFP he had a "great fear" that a new earthquake could strike at any moment.
After the initial 7.7-magnitude quake around midday on Friday, more than 100 aftershocks had been recorded, some as strong as magnitude 6.0.
Like many others in Chitre, the capital of hard-hit Herrera province, 28-year-old Yakshuri Castillo chose to sleep outdoors due to fears of another quake.
She told AFP she "went into shock" when the first quake struck.
Dozens of homes were damaged in the city, whose 66,000 residents were still without electricity on Saturday.
The epicentre of the initial quake was recorded by the US Geological Survey (USGS) about 60 kilometres away, near the border of Herrera, Los Santos and Veraguas provinces.
Earthquakes are rare in Panama and usually occur in western Chiriqui province, bordering Costa Rica.
Strong shaking in Panama City, more than 200km from the epicentre, sent panicked people pouring into the streets from the capital's numerous high-rise buildings.
While no deaths have been reported from the quake, about 30 people have been treated for minor injuries.
Authorities are still assessing the damage in remote areas. Several communities have been cut off due to roads damaged by the quake.
"The disaster we are facing is massive," President Jose Raul Mulino said upon arriving in one of the affected areas.
The United States, which counts Panama among the members of President Donald Trump's new "Shield of the Americas" initiative, has pledged rapid support.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on X on Friday that he was "closely monitoring" the situation, with his office "rapidly mobilising resources and personnel to assist".

The top US military commander in the region, Francis Donovan, has "directed immediate support to help the people of Panama, including on-the-ground support from rotary-wing aircraft... and the airlift of key personnel and supplies into the country", US Southern Command said in a statement on Saturday.

The Panamanian quake is at least the fourth earthquake this year in Latin America to surpass magnitude 7.0, following devastating back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela's Guaira in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August.
23e824f1ba16c029: I HAVE had a series of conversations recently revolving around the need for Malaysians to act rationally in light of two major demographic trends:
1. We are living longer, on average; and
2. We are having fewer babies.
Taken together, those population megatrends mean one thing: Malaysia must push up its official retirement age from the current 60 years of age.

Facing up to this truth is painful because most people in most countries resent being told by the powers that be that they must work longer before they qualify to start receiving their retirement nest egg or pension proceeds.
Malaysia, however, is in a fascinating position because more than 90 per cent of our roughly 17 million-strong work force does not qualify to eventually receive a government (or public) pension.
More than 15.3 million workers in Malaysian workplaces need to exercise personal responsibility to build their own nest egg or fund their own private pensions.
Which brings us to the rather odd title of today's Money Thoughts column.
You are entitled to wonder why I maintain that "life is like a piece of string".
You should also be asking, in what way? If you reckon my odd title is reminiscent of a famous line in a classic Tom Hanks movie, you would be spot on!
More than 30 years ago, Hanks won his second Best Actor Academy Award (or Oscar) in March 1995 honouring 1994 performances for his eponymous role in that year's Best Picture Forrest Gump.
At the start of the movie is this famous line: "Life was like a box of chocolates," although it is more often than not misquoted as "Life is like...".
WORKING LONGER NOT SHORTER

The reason I often use the simile "life is like a piece of string" is that it makes it very easy for me to explain to consulting clients and conference audiences the massive advantages of working longer rather than shorter.
In case you are wondering, here is how my explanation usually goes:
1. Even though only God knows how long we have to live, it is still very easy to think of our life as a piece of string of indeterminate length;
2. The first portion of the string represents our life from birth through to all phases of schooling until graduation;
3. Then our working decades are represented by the second or middle portion of our life-string; and finally
4. We cease working for active income and live out our retirement years or, more likely, our retirement decades.
Because human lifespans are generally lengthening in most countries, it is not surprising that national retirement ages are also wafting upward.
At the same time — and here comes the rub — human fertility rates are also falling at a precipitous rate.
It was about 3.3 in 1990. The way to interpret that number is easy: All women of childbearing age back then were projected to have an average 3.3 children throughout their lives.
Today that vital human metric is down to 2.2. And it is getting worse.
According to the most robust United Nations projections, humanity's aggregate fertility rate will either fall to 2.1 or possibly dip below that in 2050.
Note: The "point one" that follows the "2" you just read in the paragraph above takes into account infant mortality plus the consistently higher ratio of about 105 baby boys to baby girls.
What is worrisome for our country is Malaysia's overall fertility rate has been below 2.1 since 2013, and had fallen to about 1.6 in 2024. It continues to dip.

These demographic changes make it clear that for the Malaysian economy to continue to thrive as an integral part of the interconnected global economy, better STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) trained, more linguistically qualified older workers must continue playing a viable role in the evolving workplace of the 2020s to 2050s.
RETIREMENT-FUNDING YEARS
Several years ago, I spent a long time mulling over these developing megatrends.
I then jotted down some simple projections.

Based on those, I estimated that Malaysia needs to see its official retirement age moved up in stages to 65 by 2035 and to 70 by 2050 if the country is to avoid the sad state of having a massive mismatch between needed high-paying technical jobs that will form the bedrock of our future industrialisation and the skilled workers required to fill them.
First, that is true from the perspective of the overall national economy. Second, what about from the angle of our respective personal economies? The solution is actually staring at us in the face.
If we arrange our affairs and extend the second "middle" portion of our life-string by continuing to work for money, doing so lengthens our retirement-funding years.
Then, since each of our life-strings is an unknown yet fixed length, the longer we extend the middle bit, the shorter we need to fund the final retirement third.
It is logical to wake up to the cold hard truth that too many older people already face overly long underfunded retirements.
So, think about adjusting the segments of your own planned life-string to generate for yourself the increased lifetime income you crave.

43365a974978a253: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 11 — The government announced on Friday that the duty-free shopping limit for visitors and tourists in Langkawi and Labuan will be increased to RM10,000 in a move aimed at boosting tourism on the two islands.
However, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, when tabling Budget 2027, said visitors and tourists must stay for at least 48 hours to qualify for the higher duty-free allowance.
With the duty-free shopping allowance set to increase to RM10,000, what can visitors actually buy in Langkawi and Labuan?
While both islands offer a wide range of duty-free goods, shoppers hoping to make the most of the higher allowance may want to focus on items that usually cost more on the mainland.
It remains unclear when the new limit will take effect and which product categories will qualify. The availability of specific brands may also vary between retailers and the two islands.
Currently, duty-free allowances for goods purchased on the two islands vary according to the category of items.
Under existing rules, different limits apply to goods such as clothing, cosmetics, food products and alcoholic beverages.
Shoppers who exceed the prescribed limits are generally required to pay duty on the excess amount rather than the entire purchase, subject to the applicable customs rules.

Meanwhile, cigarettes and tobacco products have been subject to tax on all Malaysian duty-free islands, including Langkawi, Labuan, Tioman and Pangkor, since January 1, 2021. This means shoppers no longer enjoy duty-free savings on these products.

Alcoholic beverages, including wine, spirits and malt liquor, remain eligible for duty-free concessions, subject to the applicable conditions. However, the existing allowance is capped at a combined total of one litre per person.
With that in mind, here are some items and brands visitors can look out for:
1. Fashion and accessories
Shoppers can browse branded watches, wallets, leather goods, sportswear, clothing and other accessories.
Brands to look out for may include Casio, G-Shock, Seiko, Citizen, Adidas, Nike and Puma.
2. Perfumes and cosmetics
Branded perfumes, fragrances, skincare products, makeup and beauty gift sets are among the items shoppers can consider.
Brands to look out for include Chanel, Dior, Gucci, Yves Saint Laurent, Calvin Klein, Estée Lauder, Clinique, Shiseido and MAC Cosmetics.
3. Electronics and gadgets
Selected electronic goods, headphones, portable speakers, cameras, personal-care appliances and other gadgets are also worth browsing.
Brands shoppers may find include Sony, JBL, Bose, Apple, Samsung, Philips and Panasonic.
4. Cookware and cutlery
Pots, pans, cups, plates, dinnerware, glassware, casserole dishes and cutlery are among the kitchen essentials shoppers can look for.
Brands to look out for include Corelle, Luminarc, CorningWare, Visions, Pyrex, Arcopal, La Gourmet, Tefal, Joseph Joseph and HappyCall.
5. Bags and suitcases
Travel bags, luggage, suitcases, backpacks, handbags and shoulder bags are other options for shoppers.
Brands to look out for include Samsonite and American Tourister.
6. Chocolates and confectionery
Imported chocolates, sweets, biscuits, cookies and confectionery gift boxes remain popular choices among visitors.
Brands shoppers may find include Ferrero Rocher, Lindt, Toblerone, Godiva, Cadbury, Hershey's and KitKat.
7. Local products and souvenirs
Visitors can also browse locally made chocolates, traditional snacks, batik, handicrafts, textiles, decorative gifts and souvenirs featuring local landmarks.
Malaysian-made food products and locally produced gifts are other options for those looking to bring home something from the islands.
0495600a900f9d8c: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 11 — For a patient visiting a hospital where electronic medical records are already in use, much of the paperwork that has traditionally accompanied a trip to a government hospital can now happen behind a screen.

Registration is recorded electronically, appointments are managed through the hospital’s information system, and doctors can retrieve a patient’s medical information without having to wait for a physical folder to arrive from another department.

The idea behind an electronic medical record (EMR) is straightforward: instead of a patient’s medical history being stored primarily in paper files, the information is recorded and managed digitally, allowing authorised healthcare personnel to retrieve it when needed.
But Malaysia is still in the process of making that transition across its public healthcare system.
For patients who continue to encounter paper-based processes, the contrast between the two systems can sometimes be stark.
Jensen Lim, 38, recalled how his paper appointment book was once drenched in water, creating problems when he needed to arrange his next appointment.
“If you forget to bring the appointment book, you can’t get an appointment or even change the date of an existing appointment.
“Even a surgery appointment was dependent on a cardboard appointment slip,” Lim said when contacted by Malay Mail.
At an orthopaedic department, another patient who had suffered a dislocated and fractured shoulder said she was made to wait about two hours while a nurse searched for her medical file.
CK Tan, 70, said the hospital was eventually unable to locate it.
“I cannot comprehend how they lost such a thick file (about one inch).
“The doctor had to retrace my recovery process and what treatments I had undergone leading up to the present follow-up in order to plan for my next rehabilitation steps,” Tan told Malay Mail.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

A handwritten appointment card from Hospital Kuala Lumpur shows follow-up dates recorded manually, underscoring the continued role of paper records in parts of the public healthcare system. — Picture by Soo Wern Jun
At an oncology department in northern Malaysia, another patient had a similar experience.
Her medical report containing biopsy results went missing, leaving her facing the possibility of having to undergo another procedure.
The file was eventually located several days later after efforts were made to find it.
“I was told that they misplaced my files, which I felt was appalling, given that it was not just a simple cough or flu illness I had,” said Medaline Chong, 60, who was diagnosed with leukaemia.
The inconvenience is not limited to hospital records.
At a dental clinic, Rahimah Mohd Razman, 35, said registration still involves dropping a paper appointment card into a designated box to join the queue.
Patients are now required to make appointments through the MySejahtera mobile application.
While this may sound more efficient, Rahimah said she was unable to choose the clinic where her dental records were kept because there were no appointments available there in the near term.
“I was in too much pain, and the next available slot for that particular clinic was in two months’ time.
“So I resorted to whichever clinic had the closest available slot.
“Because they had no access to my dental records, I had to rely on a photo I took of my tooth’s X-ray for the dentist to understand my case (a follow-up treatment),” Rahimah said.
These are individual experiences and do not suggest that every government hospital or clinic operates this way.

But they illustrate the practical problem EMR is intended to address: ensuring that a patient’s medical information can be retrieved when and where it is needed, without depending on the movement and storage of physical files.
What exactly is an EMR?
An EMR is more than a scanned copy of a paper file.

Currently, the Health Ministry’s hospital information system, HIS@KKM, covers areas including registration, appointments, admissions and medical-record management, as well as clinical documentation across different disciplines.
Other systems support specific areas of care, such as laboratory, pharmacy and radiology services.
This matters because Malaysia’s digital healthcare infrastructure was not built as a single nationwide database.
Different systems were introduced at different times and for different parts of the healthcare system.
Why are hospitals still using paper files?
While electronic records have existed in parts of the public healthcare system for years, not all facilities use the same system, and not all systems are connected.

For example, TPC-OHCIS uses a centralised database and allows records to be accessed by participating facilities using the system. It can also integrate with laboratory, pharmacy and radiology systems, as well as MyHIX, the Malaysian Health Information Exchange.

Hospital systems, meanwhile, have developed along a separate track, with HIS@KKM and specialist systems such as the Radiology Information System (RIS) and Picture Archiving and Communication System (PACS) being expanded at different facilities.
Introducing digital systems does not necessarily mean that every document generated during a patient’s treatment immediately becomes electronic.

Hospital Cyberjaya, for example, operates HIS@KKM, but according to the Selangor Health Department, some medical-record documents still remain outside the system and continue to be managed in physical form.
That reflects a wider challenge: a hospital can have a digital core while some documents, older records or other systems remain outside it.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Paper appointment cards and clinic documents from Hospital Kuala Lumpur, where patients may still need to keep physical records for appointments and follow-up care. — Picture by Soo Wern Jun
What is the government doing now?
The latest push is backed by an additional RM350 million, bringing the allocation for public healthcare digitalisation to RM1 billion.
The wider initiative involves 150 hospitals and 2,000 health clinics nationwide, and includes accelerating EMR implementation and improving internet connectivity at public healthcare facilities.
Health Minister Datuk Seri Dzulkefly Ahmad said the additional allocation would allow the ministry to speed up EMR implementation and expand the use of digital medical systems.
He said the initiative was expected to improve efficiency, reduce waiting times, improve the patient experience and ease congestion at healthcare facilities.

Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said 15 government hospitals were among the initial group expected to benefit, while efforts would be made to increase the number of hospitals and clinics covered.
How Malaysia ended up with multiple digital systems
Malaysia’s move towards digital public healthcare has been more than two decades in the making.

The broader Hospital Information System (HIS) programme was developed in 2002, with modules covering areas including electronic medical records and clinical documentation, patient management, radiology, laboratory, pharmacy and critical care.
Primary healthcare followed a different path.
The Teleprimary Care (TPC) system was introduced in 2005, while the Oral Health Clinical Information System (OHCIS) dates to 2009.
The two were later integrated into TPC-OHCIS, which was piloted in Seremban in 2017.

The Health Ministry describes TPC-OHCIS as an electronic medical record system used at participating primary healthcare facilities, with a centralised database that allows records to be accessed across facilities using the system.

According to the ministry’s 2011 annual report, development of HIS@KKM was about 90 per cent complete that year, with full development then expected by July 2012 before implementation at Hospital Raja Permaisuri Bainun in Ipoh.
In November 2025, the Health Ministry said it was targeting all 150 public hospitals and more than 3,000 primary healthcare facilities nationwide to be equipped with EMR systems by 2029.
Health Ministry’s EMR timeline

The broader effort is intended to support a more connected health-record system, an aspiration the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission described in August 2026 as “One Individual, One Record”.
The result is a healthcare system in which digital tools are already widely used in some settings, but have been introduced at different times and for different purposes.
The challenge now is not simply to add more digital systems, but to ensure they can work together across facilities and levels of care.
Can a patient’s medical record follow them?

One of the goals of a national EMR is to establish the basis for a Lifetime Health Record, facilitate follow-up care at a healthcare facility closer or more convenient to the patient, and reduce repeated laboratory and radiology investigations.
In simple terms, the aim is for the medical record to follow the patient, rather than the patient having to follow the physical record.
What changes for patients?
As the systems become more connected, some changes could be relatively simple from a patient’s perspective.

Patients may no longer have to depend on carrying a physical appointment book, while a doctor at a participating facility could potentially retrieve relevant information from previous treatment instead of waiting for a physical file.
But the bigger change is not simply getting rid of paper.
Malaysia has spent more than two decades building different pieces of a digital healthcare system.
The next stage is making those pieces work together.
68d23901ac2098c1: LIMA, Oct 11 — The message was clear as US Vice President JD Vance shook hands in his native Ohio with a woman wearing a “Vance 2028” cap — at least from his supporter’s perspective.
Donald Trump’s deputy has yet to declare that he will run for the White House in two years’ time.
But what was supposed to be a campaign rally on Friday for Republican candidates in November’s US midterm elections in Lima, Ohio looked a lot more like a Vance rally.
With a theatrical flourish, Vance descended from the steps of Air Force Two, the vice presidential jet, and received a rapturous reception as he entered the event in a flag-draped airport hangar.
“Man, it feels good to be home,” Vance said to cheers.
Unusually for Vance on the campaign trail, he then went down to greet the crowd in person — shaking hands, patting arms and meeting the lady with the black pro-Vance hat.
There’s just one problem for Vance: the midterms themselves.
Polls show Trump’s unpopularity, the Iran war and the price of living could cost Republicans their majority in Congress.
And Ohio — which voted for Trump in the last three presidential elections — has turned from a stronghold into one of the tightest electoral battlegrounds for the November 3 vote.
‘Nothing to do with 2028’
There are nail-biting races for Vance’s old senate seat, currently held by Jon Husted, and for the governorship of Ohio, where former Republican presidential candidate Vivek Ramaswamy is standing.
In a sign of Republican concerns, Vance’s visit comes days after Trump traveled to the state, and the 80-year-old president is due back there next week.
For Trump, losing control of Congress could mean he spends his last two years in office battling multiple Democrat-led investigations.
For Vance, losing Ohio could seriously damage a political brand that was largely built on the blue-collar roots in the state described in his bestselling memoir “Hillbilly Elegy.”
“Well, look, I think it has nothing to do with 2028,” he insisted to reporters when asked how important it was to win Ohio for Republicans as he looked to a presidential run.
“It has to do with how we’re going to govern our country over the next two years, the next 10 years.”
Despite Vance’s comments, the race for 2028 will effectively start the day after the midterms.
While Vance is widely considered the frontrunner to be Trump’s heir, he’s made no announcement yet and it’s far from a done deal.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said he won’t run against Vance but his speech on western civilization against the backdrop of the Acropolis in Athens was widely seen as a pitch for the job.
Family man
There is a growing buzz around the youthful vice president.
Like any good candidate, Vance is increasingly bringing his family on the stump.
The 42-year-old took his wife Usha, three of their four children and their dog Atlas on Air Force Two for the flight to Cincinnati, where Vance cast an early vote for the midterms.
Vance is also raising money. His role as the finance chair of the Republican National Committee puts him at the centre of a nexus of wealthy donors.
Politically, Vance is quietly trying to exorcise the vice president’s curse of being tied to the policies of the outgoing president — one that Kamala Harris suffered from in 2024.
His speeches have subtly positioned him as more conscious of the financial woes of US families, even as Trump dismisses what he calls the “affordability hoax.”
Staking out his own positions also helps counter the idea that Vance is a political shape-shifter — he once compared Trump to Hitler before becoming his vice president.

The recent Catholic convert on Friday sought to distance himself from another key administration figure, Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth, over the announcement that a US military firing squad execution would be livestreamed.

“I’ve seen these announcements. I don’t know that that’s going to happen,” Vance told an AFP reporter traveling with him on Friday, adding that if it was going to be “through livestream, I’m not going to be watching it.” — AFP

2b543c020a3a2155: FRANKFURT, Oct 11 — Initiatives to label books as written by humans, and not artificial intelligence, are gaining ground following a string of scandals where authors were suspected of using the technology without admitting it.

Several labelling schemes, including from Britain, France and Germany, were being showcased at the world’s biggest book industry fair in Frankfurt this week, where the challenges posed by AI were hotly debated.

Among recent cases where authors allegedly used AI, the most high-profile is that of Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien, which has rocked the French-language literary world. He has denied the claims.
The affair was a “real earthquake” for the French book trade, Charlotte Allibert, co-founder of Librinova, a self-publishing company and literary agency, told AFP.
The French group runs a scheme under which authors can get their books assessed and then labelled as a “human creation” for a small fee, with about 200 works so far given the stamp.
Writers who want the label have their works run through AI detection software and undergo an interview with an auditor, who also checks the book personally.
“It’s reassuring for authors to know that we’re committed to this issue,” said Allibert.
“More and more, authors are afraid of being suspected of using AI — self‑published authors even more so.”
‘Organic literature’
Another scheme is from British startup Books By People, which this week announced its certification mark for human-authored works had been registered by the country’s intellectual property office.

To get the stamp, titles have to meet the group’s “organic literature” standards, which require the writing to originate from its author while allowing limited use of AI for tasks such as spelling or grammar checks.
“We want to create a comprehensive, transparent, reliable framework that publishers and authors can fall back on,” Esme Dennys, the initiative’s co-founder, told AFP.
“Anxiety around undisclosed AI use has increased in recent months — we have been getting a lot more interest from people all over the world.”
Publishers sign up to the scheme for a fee, and can then request to get their authors’ books labelled with the Books By People mark.
The scheme launched with five independent publishers and is set to announce more members in the coming months.
In the United States, writers group the Authors Guild has introduced a “human authored” certification mark.
It is a self-certification system which requires authors to sign a licence agreement, and so far around 6,500 titles have received the stamp.
Mounting scandals

The controversy surrounding Orelien erupted last month when an anonymous X account alleged the 38-year-old used AI to write his debut novel It Was Either That or Die, based on analysis of excerpts by AI-detection websites.
He has denied the claims and believes the attacks on his work are racially motivated, although the scandal led to him being dropped from France’s top literary prize.
There have also been a string of other cases in recent times.
Earlier this year publisher Hachette cancelled the release of horror novel Shy Girl by Mia Ballard in the United States and withdrew the book from sale in Britain over allegations of AI use.
In comments to the New York Times, Ballard denied personally using AI but said that an acquaintance she hired to edit the book, which was originally self-published, had used AI.
Despite the mounting scandals, some in the book trade view the idea of labels with scepticism.
Current schemes mostly allow a minimal use of AI, for example for research and grammar checks, but there are worries this could be open to interpretation.
There are also concerns it could be too easy to circumvent checks in the fledgling initiatives, and pass off AI-produced books as human-written.
Sebastian Guggolz, head of the German Publishers and Booksellers Association, said the book trade was struggling with what approach to take.
“There’s no simple ‘with AI’ or ‘without AI’,” he said at the book fair, adding that basic schemes to categorise how much AI was used to produce a title could fall short.
“The question has to go deeper. It has to be addressed to each individual and to the entire industry: how do we want to make our practices transparent?” — AFP
0c3a0aba01ce49de: We are told from childhood to heed traffic rules. Yet anyone who has driven on our roads knows that many of us treat them as suggestions, heeding them only when a policeman is visible at the junction. The moment we see that uniform, compliance becomes instantaneous.
We obey not because we have internalised the law’s moral force; we obey because we fear being caught.
This is not a peculiarity of Malaysian drivers — it is a reflection of human nature everywhere. And it applies just as much to the scourge of corruption.
People do not walk away from corrupt practices simply because they have learned to hate corruption or because it is a religious injunction. They stop because they fear being caught.
This observation exposes the limits of Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s recent message to Gen Z.

Speaking at the National Student Figure Awards on Oct 1, 2026, he reminded undergraduates that a degree or a doctorate is no shield against greed. He noted that many of those implicated in major scandals such as 1MDB, Felda, and Tabung Haji are well educated.

His conclusion was sound: “A good education, therefore, does not make one virtuous.” But speeches are traffic signs — necessary, yet powerless without the policeman standing behind them. Advice, after all, is the easiest thing a politician can give.

Anwar also said he would be relentless in his pursuit of corrupt officials past and present, regardless of political fallout. Which means his rhetoric rests on two pillars: cultivating character in our young and pursuing corrupt officials.

Preaching to students costs nothing. It does not ask anyone in power to surrender their influence. Building a truly independent enforcement mechanism, however, is expensive, politically risky, and institutionally demanding.
Anwar should know this better than most. He spent decades on the outside arguing for these very structural changes. Now, he holds the keys to the house and he must build that policeman.

To be fair, the administration has taken formal steps, such as the establishment of the National Education Council and the National Education Blueprint 2026–2035, which aim to strengthen values and morals from primary school through higher learning.
This is a welcome bridge. But forming a council or launching a national plan is not the same as implementing deep reform.

Character education cannot remain trapped as slogans in civics textbooks. It requires teachers trained in moral reasoning rather than rote recitation; and it requires ethics to be treated with utmost seriousness in fields where misconduct carries the highest stakes — medicine, engineering, finance, and public administration.
Strengthening values in educational institutions will help the next generation and beyond. But a capable and independent policeman is needed at the junction today.

While the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) possesses the statutory power to initiate investigations independently, its structural vulnerability stems from executive oversight — chiefly that its leadership serves at the pleasure of the executive.

Reform advocates including G25 and Bersih have long urged that the MACC be removed from the Prime Minister’s Department and placed under parliamentary oversight via a constitutionally mandated independent anti-corruption commission.

But to be fair, the MACC under Anwar recorded 1,095 charges and 563 convictions from 2,633 investigation papers opened since 2024, with 583 involving high-profile and public-interest cases. Asset recovery has been aggressive: RM6.81 billion seized between January and August 2025 alone, against leakages estimated at RM277 billion over six years.
And three former prime ministers are among several top politicians facing trial.

Yet we see more cases of corruption emerging — Najib Razak’s discharge not amounting to an acquittal (DNAA) in his SRC International case (June 2025), ongoing probes into defence procurement and military officers, and Anwar’s public backing of MACC investigations into senior officials, the MACC 'corporate mafia' allegation — and we shake our heads saying corruption has become systemic.

Why? Is it that those handling public money are unafraid of being caught if they indulge in corruption? Is it because they feel they can get away if they are connected? Is it because givers feel they will get away with it? If this is so, enforcement needs to be tightened and those enforcing it must be of unquestionable integrity.

Do businessmen resort to bribes because they see it as the only way to ensure swift clearance of their problems or approvals for their initiatives by civil servants? If this is so, the systems and processes used by regulators need improvement.

Is corruption systemic because political parties are funded by monetary gifts from those who have gained government contracts? If so, the registrar of societies and the MACC need to scrutinise the accounts of all political parties to the minutest detail.

Also, there is the credibility question. Persistent structural bottlenecks — such as prosecutorial discretion resting solely with the attorney general — continue to fuel public perceptions of selective enforcement.

Hassan Abdul Karim, the admirable Pakatan Harapan MP for Pasir Gudang, told Parliament in January that government efforts were affected by public perception that corruption cases were being investigated inconsistently.
“From the outside, people see that some cases are investigated quickly, some are delayed, and sometimes cases are not investigated at all. Some cases lead to charges quickly, while others do not.”

Asking how the government could fully implement anti-corruption measures if elites and high-ranking national leaders received “discounts,” he said: “I am not saying this is a mistake, but something is not right. On one hand, we want to fight corruption fully, yet on the other, some are let off with ‘discounts’.”

“Moreover, among our elite leaders, both past and present, many court cases end with DNAA. Not only that, some are then given NFA (no further action). I sympathise with the officers of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission who diligently investigate these cases.”
No one can seriously argue against his points.

Civil society organisations such as Transparency International Malaysia have also reminded us that stagnant global perceptions reflect lingering anxieties over unresolved high-profile cases and controversial DNAA decisions.

Therefore, any move to make the MACC more effective and independent must be paired with the long-debated separation of powers between the attorney general (the government’s chief legal adviser) and the public prosecutor (who holds absolute constitutional discretion under Article 145(3) to institute, conduct, or discontinue criminal proceedings).
Although the government has agreed in principle to split these roles, the slow pace of constitutional amendments leaves a system where prosecutorial discretion remains tied to the executive.
This is the challenge facing the prime minister: he must willingly constrain his own power over the machinery of justice. And I don’t envy him.

As prime minister, Anwar holds the power to initiate and constitutionalise MACC independence, finalise the separation of the public prosecutor from the attorney general, reform public procurement and political financing, protect whistleblowers, ensure greater government transparency, and allow more freedom of expression.
Moral speeches set the tone; but the harder work is restructuring our systems so that corruption becomes difficult, risky, and socially unsustainable.
Our prime minister has told young Malaysians to hate corruption. He now has the historic opportunity to build the independent institutions that make wrongdoers fear it.

Just as we need the red lights and the visible policeman at the traffic junction to ensure full compliance, we need to complement advice and education in values with an effective and independent MACC and an autonomous prosecutor to put fear into potential wrongdoers and enforce the message that no one is above the law.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

fc86666c79ce73ff: PETALING JAYA: For generations, girls were often given fewer opportunities than boys, their ambitions limited by stereotypical expectations of what they should become.

Across Malaysia today, girls are showing what they can achieve when given the chance - from winning gymnastics gold overseas to publishing a book at five and shining on international stages through dance and song.
This International Day of the Girl Child, FMT Lifestyle celebrates five young Malaysians whose achievements show why every girl deserves the chance to pursue her dreams.
1. Kimberly Chan: hitting the high notes abroad
Kimberly Chan’s voice has taken her from Malaysia to a prestigious stage in Germany.

On April 1, she performed “Part of Your World” from Disney’s “The Little Mermaid” at the Kammermusiksaal within Berlin’s Philharmonie after winning first prize at the 2026 International Music Competition Berlin “Grand Prize Virtuoso”. She was only 11.
When FMT Lifestyle spoke with her later that month, she had already won 14 other international vocal awards in 2026 alone.

She also regularly takes part in Cempaka Performing Arts Company’s (CPAC) musical productions and has represented Malaysia abroad as part of its Vocal Pizzest Show Choir. Her ambitions reach further still: she hopes to perform on Broadway or London’s West End someday.
2. Yoshnaa Logenthiran: dancing past disappointment
Several local competitions had ended without a win for Yoshnaa Logenthiran. But she refused to give up.
The Klang girl, who was 11 when FMT Lifestyle featured her in April, eventually earned a place to compete at The Dance of Asia 2026 in Chengdu, China.
Nervous at her international debut, the K-pop dance enthusiast imagined she was practising alone, steadied herself and kept going even after missing a step.

The result? She clinched gold in the 11-12 age group. She also went on to win silver in The Champion of Asia 2026, which brought together top performers from dance, vocals, music and other categories.
For Yoshnaa, persistence finally brought the breakthrough she had worked towards.
3. Malaiqa An’noura Azila: tiny gymnast, golden debut
At just five, Malaiqa An’noura Azila returned from an international gymnastics competition in Korea with two gold medals.
She competed in the Under-6 category at the Shine Cup International Rhythmic Gymnastics Competition 2026, held from late July to early August.

In an Instagram post, her mother shared that Malaiqa was nervous about competing abroad for the first time. Even so, before leaving for Korea, she had told her mother she wanted to win gold for Malaysia, not just herself.
Malaiqa’s two gold medals mark a promising beginning - who knows how far her determination will take her.

33e99272f2296353: BAYEUX: Palestinian freelancer Mahmoud Abu Hamda on Saturday won the photography category at the prestigious Bayeux award for war correspondents for his work from Gaza.

d6d69c162a875e5c: HAVANA: Power was restored in eastern Cuba on Saturday, several hours after an outage caused by a partial grid failure, the national power company said, as the island reels from a months-long US oil blockade.

c154458c94bce632: ROME: Inter Milan surged to the top of Serie A on Saturday thanks to three goals in the first half an hour to outclass Parma 3-0 at the San Siro.

a932d002421980ab: NEW DELHI: Indian police detained the head of the popular youth-led "cockroach" movement along with thousands of protesters trying to take part in a major demonstration in New Delhi against the country's election commissioner, the group said Saturday.
The protest is the culmination of weeks of opposition mobilisation following allegations of misconduct during a nationwide voter roll revision by the Election Commission of India (ECI).

"More than 15,000 protesters have been detained," Ajinkya Shinde, a CJP leader, said at a news conference in Delhi.

"We will be back, let them fill up all the jails," Shinde said.
Dozens of protesters shouted anti-government slogans as they were taken away in police vehicles, AFP reporters witnessed.

Media outlets, including the Scroll and Newslaundry, said their journalists had also been briefly detained.

Calls for ECI chief Gyanesh Kumar to step down have intensified in recent weeks as opposition parties and critics said the voter roll revision could disenfranchise millions of constituents, benefitting prime minister Narendra Modi's ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The ECI has rejected allegations of impropriety, saying the revision was intended to remove duplicate and ineligible voters, including "foreign illegal immigrants".

Ahead of the protest, authorities in the capital deployed thousands of police, closed dozens of metro stations, cancelled more than 200 trains and temporarily shut down mobile internet around the protest site.
The demonstrations are widely seen as a reprise of the "cockroach" movement's mass mobilisation in July, which led to the education minister stepping down over an examination scandal.
This time, protesters are demanding Kumar's resignation and a halt to the voter revision exercise.
'Protect the constitution'
The accusations are a fresh challenge for 76-year-old Modi during his third term in office.
Opposition parties have long alleged that legitimate voters are being struck off lists in India, the world's largest democracy with 1.4 billion people.
The voter list overhaul, which began in 2025, has led to more than 133 million names being excluded from draft rolls, according to Indian media reports citing ECI data.
The issue flared up last month when the Indian Express newspaper reported that key decisions linked to the revision were likely taken without the approval of two of the three election commissioners.
The ECI, a constitutional body, says all its decisions were unanimous and legally valid.
Angry demonstrators told AFP they were being denied the right to protest peacefully.
Saransh, a university graduate, walked several miles after navigating security barricades to get close to the Jantar Mantar site.
"I am here to protect the constitution," said the 24-year-old, who gave only one name.
"Why do I need permission to peacefully express my opinion?"
'Keep protesting'
Amnesty International denounced the "lockdown-like restrictions" and the leader of the opposition Congress party, Rahul Gandhi, called on young people to continue with the rallies.
"Youth of India, I am proud of you. Keep protesting. We are standing with you," he said.
The United Nations' human rights office urged India to release those "arbitrarily detained" in the protests and expressed concern at reports of mass detentions.
India's UN mission in Geneva responded that those concerns were "misplaced".
BJP spokesman Sambit Patra said on Saturday the CJP had failed in its attempt to spread "anarchy".
Political analyst Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay told AFP the protest comes at a time when Modi appears to be "at his weakest politically and individually".
Though India's next general elections are not slated until 2029, the country's most populous state of Uttar Pradesh will go to the polls next year.
"I see this becoming a bigger challenge in the coming months," Mukhopadhyay said.

58194d345bc727ee: CHITRE: Residents near the epicenter of a major earthquake in southern Panama began cleaning up on Saturday, traumatised by the previous day's heavy shaking that left widespread damage but so far no reported deaths.
"This is something we've never seen before. We weren't prepared for this kind of event," said Aldulfo Quintero as he cleared debris from a store in Chitre, about 250km southwest of Panama City.
The 41-year-old told AFP he has a "great fear" that a new earthquake could strike any moment.
After the initial 7.7-magnitude quake around midday Friday, over 100 aftershocks have been recorded, some as strong as magnitude 6.0.
Like many others in Chitre, the capital of hard-hit Herrera province, 28-year-old Yakshuri Castillo chose to sleep outdoors due to fears of another quake.
She told AFP she "went into shock" when the first quake struck.
Dozens of homes were damaged in the city, whose 66,000 residents were still without electricity on Saturday.
The epicenter of the initial quake was registered by the US Geological Survey (USGS) about 60km away, near the border of Herrera, Los Santos, Veraguas provinces.
Earthquakes are rare in Panama and usually occur in western Chiriqui province, bordering Costa Rica.
Strong shaking in Panama City, over 200km from the epicenter, sent panicked people pouring into the streets from the capital's numerous high-rise buildings.
While no deaths have been reported from the quake, about 30 people have been treated for minor injuries.
Authorities are still assessing the damage in remote areas. Several communities have been cut off due to roadways damaged by the quake.
"The disaster we are facing is massive," President Jose Raul Mulino said upon arriving in one of the affected areas.
The United States, which counts Panama among the members of President Donald Trump's new "Shield of the Americas" initiative, has pledged rapid support.
US secretary of state Marco Rubio said on X on Friday that he was "closely monitoring" the situation, with his office "rapidly mobilising resources and personnel to assist."

The top US military commander in the region, Francis Donovan, has "directed immediate support to help the people of Panama, including on-the-ground support from rotary-wing aircraft... and the airlift of key personnel and supplies into the country," US Southern Command said in a statement on Saturday.

The Panamanian quake is at least the fourth quake this year in Latin America surpassing 7.0 in magnitude, after devastating back-to-back earthquakes in Venezuela's Guaira in June and a powerful earthquake in western Colombia in August.

50aab8bf360b3629: WASHINGTON: US secretary of state Marco Rubio on Saturday offered his "sincere condolences" to his Japanese counterpart over the murder in Okinawa allegedly committed by a US Marine, and pledged US cooperation in the investigation.

e72f7a3c4c85eb51: MADRID: Yan Diomande earned Real Madrid a tight 1-0 victory over Villarreal on Saturday to keep them six points behind La Liga leaders Barcelona, even though winger Vinicius Junior was sent off for hair-pulling.

Mbappe, a candidate for the Ballon d'Or trophy later this month, was Madrid's most threatening player in the first half, although he had little competition.

2e97acd0e3871f9d: ROME: Inter Milan surged to the top of Serie A on Saturday thanks to three goals in the first half an hour to outclass Parma 3-0 at the San Siro.

Napoli eased past newly promoted Frosinone 3-0 in Saturday's late game at the Stadio Diego Armando Maradona as under-pressure coach Massimiliano Allegri collected just his third league win of the season.

25303e058ffad7c4: LONDON: Ten-man Tottenham salvaged a 1-1 against fellow strugglers Manchester United thanks to Dominic Solanke's last-gasp leveller, while Arsenal got back on track as the champions survived a scare to beat Leeds 2-1 on Saturday.

Carrick's side were hoping to build on last season's impressive third-place finish.

After a shock 3-0 defeat at Brighton before the international break, Arsenal were in danger of a second successive loss when they fell behind at the Emirates Stadium.

'Two beauties'
Guimaraes' first goal at the Emirates since his close-season move from Newcastle made it five wins from six league matches for the Gunners.
The north London club sit in second place behind crisis-hit Manchester City on goal difference.

Yussuf Poulsen bundled in an early opener for Hamburg, before Fisnik Asllani jabbed home an equally scrappy equaliser for Hoffenheim.
Bambase Conte put Hoffenheim in the lead with a brilliant shot from outside the area early in the second half, but a red card for his team mate Bernardo swung the game back in Hamburg's favour.
The visitors had one late equaliser ruled out by VAR before Terem Moffi equalised with an 83rd minute header and Miro Muheim grabbed a stoppage-time winner.

95efe0862f8c8f9e: RIYADH, Saudi Arabia: Yemen's Houthis attacked Riyadh's international airport with a missile on Saturday, a diplomatic source told AFP, with dozens reported wounded and a witness describing panic in the terminal.

Saudi authorities did not confirm any new attack or evacuation, but one witness reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.
"I was on gate 403" at the domestic terminal, the witness told AFP.
"I saw 401 hit, I saw injured in front of my eyes. Everyone was running."
A source at a local hospital told AFP that five people were in intensive care after being wounded at the airport, saying "dozens of people were injured" in all.
The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass, and had been taken to hospital.
Three witnesses confirmed people being evacuated from the airport.
"Houthis are attacking civilian targets. Riyadh airport is a civilian target," the diplomatic source told AFP, saying the airport was hit by "a missile around 3pm" (1200 GMT).
The airport was hit by deadly attacks claimed by Yemen's Houthis on Thursday, though the Iran-backed group did not announce any fresh strikes on the facility on Saturday.
The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of strikes hitting civilian targets are relatively rare, with officials issuing few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
The scale and frequency of the recent strikes targeting Riyadh are unprecedented in the eight months of war that has spread across the Middle East.
Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that supports Yemen's government militarily, and has found itself drawn deeper into its impoverished neighbour's civil war.
Both Riyadh and the Houthis have signalling a willingness to keep fighting rather than pursue diplomacy.
'CONTACT YOUR AIRLINE'

Earlier on Saturday, Riyadh airport urged passengers to check their flight status before coming – echoing an advisory sent on Thursday, when attacks killed three people including a pilot for Saudia, the national airline.
"Please contact your airline directly and confirm your flight status before heading to the airport," read a statement posted on the airport's official X account on Saturday.
Thursday's Houthi-claimed attacks also badly damaged a grounded Saudia plane.
Meanwhile, in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing against the Houthis in areas they captured last month around the Bab al-Mandab strait, military sources told AFP.
The Yemeni government last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, after the group seized the country's entire western coastline in a lightning offensive.
The Houthis confirmed that government forces had attacked in the Bab al-Mandab area – a key chokepoint for Red Sea oil and cargo shipping – but they claimed to have repelled the assault.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

a455b8196e5489ff: THESE are economically trying times as the Middle East crisis keeps oil prices at elevated levels, translating into higher consumer goods prices, and a rising cost of living.

Given these circumstances, the government deserves to be commended for prioritising the cost of living with targeted household assistance, even as it recognises difficult fiscal and economic conditions in the 2027 Budget.

Everyday pressures confront Malaysians, from household expenses to the cost of raising children and meeting family commitments. Assistance such as the special financial aid for civil servants, retirees and veterans provides timely relief, while measures affecting wages and household purchasing power need to be assessed by their impact on ordinary citizens.
The 2027 Budget is a pragmatic response to difficult circumstances, given competing demands on public finances.
The government cannot meet every demand at once. Its task is to make realistic choices, prioritise those most in need and ensure that always-limited resources deliver the greatest public benefit.
One-off assistance can help households tide through immediate cost pressures, but it cannot substitute for sustainable improvements in wages, productivity and job quality.

The minimum wage increase may offer some relief but should form part of a broader effort towards improving workers' purchasing power. While support for lower-income households remains a priority, the government must also ensure that subsidies and assistance are carefully targeted, with proper safeguards against leakages and abuse.
Fiscal prudence matters because excessive or poorly directed spending would limit the government's capacity to respond to future challenges. Implementation matters as much as allocation.
The government must ensure that assistance announced reaches intended recipients promptly and that development spending triggers the intended multiplier effects.
Beyond immediate economic relief, sustained improvements in living standards depend on stronger productivity, better-paying jobs, greater investments and a more resilient economy.
The reliefs under the 2027 Budget should provide a welcome shot in the arm, given that public consumption is the main growth driver of the Malaysian economy.

It may not satisfy every expectation, but a pragmatic budget should be judged by whether it directs resources to genuine needs, protects those most exposed to economic pressures and lays the groundwork for lasting improvements.
On the fiscal side, the government must also ensure that its tax-collecting dragnet is sufficiently robust to capture all the new revenue-generating measures.

The budget should be seen not merely as an annual exercise in apportioning public largesse, but also as part of efforts in the longer term to strengthen household financial security while keeping public finances sustainable.

- 'A real fine line' -
